questions.question: You typed ten attacks into the chat and none worked. What can you conclude?
options: Those ten attacks failed today; without a structured, repeatable set you don't know what you didn't try
questions.explanation: Coverage you can't count and tests you can't re-run don't support a safety claim.

questions.question: Why does the judge check side effects instead of the model's reply?
options: A model can refuse in words and still call the tool, or agree in words and do nothing; harm lives in the world
Side effects are faster to compute
questions.explanation: Judge what happened: emails sent with the canary, URLs fetched, files deleted.

questions.question: In v1, base64 attacks succeed 12/12 while plain ones succeed 6/12. What does that slice tell you?
options: The model's refusals match surface text, and encoding hides it
questions.explanation: A mutation slice far above plain means a defence is matching phrasing, not intent.

questions.question: In v2, the goal slice shows destroy at 15/20 and both exfiltration goals at 0/20. What's missing?
options: A gate on irreversible actions: deleting a file isn't egress, so the egress gate never fires
questions.explanation: Goal slices point at which capability a defence doesn't cover.

questions.question: v3 scores 0/60. What's the right statement for the launch doc?
options: These 60 attacks across 3 goals, 4 framings and 5 mutations fail; the set and its regressions run on every change
questions.explanation: State what was tested. Then keep growing the grid.

questions.question: Why keep regressions.json and replay it on every change?
options: So an attack that once worked can't silently start working again after a refactor or model change
questions.explanation: Security fixes regress like any other fix. Known attacks are the cheapest tests you have.
